The Coal tit (Periparus ater) is a small-bodied passerine whose reproductive biology has been well-characterized through long-term nest-box studies across European coniferous forests. During the active metabolic phase of the breeding season, when core body temperatures reach approximately 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], females initiate their first clutch at roughly 365 days since birth [tR = roughly 365 days since birth], a timing that reflects their reliance on establishing a winter territory before breeding. The onset of reproductive capability itself is reached earlier, with puberty occurring at 57 days since birth [tp = 57 days since birth], though first breeding is typically deferred until the following spring at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. Clutch sizes in this species are notably variable, ranging from 7 to 11 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 7 to 11 eggs per clutch], a range that aligns with the moderate fecundity expected for a bird of its body size. Most populations produce a single brood annually [F_R_i = single brood annually], though second broods are occasionally recorded in years with prolonged food availability.

Hatchling development in Periparus ater proceeds rapidly under the elevated incubation temperatures maintained by the brooding female. Eggs incubated at a constant 36 °C [T = 36 °C] produce nestlings that emerge after an incubation period of approximately 16.5 days [ab = approximately 16.5 days], a duration typical for parids of similar mass. At the moment of hatching, neonates weigh only about 0.8 grams [Wwb = about 0.8 grams], reflecting the altricial condition of these birds, which are entirely dependent on parental provisioning. This initial mass is remarkably low relative to the adult body weight that will be achieved, and it underscores the intensity of the growth phase that follows. The tiny chicks, which emerge with closed eyes and sparse down, must be brooded almost continuously for the first several days to maintain thermal stability and to facilitate the absorption of residual yolk.

The nestling period of the Coal tit is characterized by an intensive growth trajectory that culminates in fledging after a relatively short developmental interval. Under the thermal conditions typical of late spring and early summer, when ambient temperatures support active metabolic functioning at approximately 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], the young depart the nest cavity at 19 days since birth [tx = 19 days since birth]. This fledging age is consistent with that of several other small parids and reflects a trade-off between the benefits of extended parental care and the increasing risk of nest predation. Upon leaving the nest, the fledglings are still dependent on adults for food delivery, though they quickly develop flight capabilities. The nestlings exhibit a rapid increase in body mass during the second week, fueled by the high-protein diet of lepidopteran larvae brought by both parents, and they attain a noticeable size by the time of nest departure.

Adult body mass in the Coal tit stabilizes at a characteristic ultimate wet weight of approximately 11.5 grams [Wwi = approximately 11.5 grams], a value that places it among the smaller members of the Paridae family. This adult mass is achieved gradually over the course of the first autumn and winter, as young birds refine their foraging efficiency on conifer seeds and spiders. The weight is maintained throughout the non-breeding season via a combination of insulating plumage and nocturnal hypothermia, which reduces daily energy expenditure. This relatively slow life-history pace, characterized by deferred first breeding and a single annual brood, is consistent with the survival strategy of a resident species occupying a predictable, though seasonally harsh, boreal niche.

Comparative physiological studies of Coal tits have revealed a series of temperature-linked developmental milestones synchronized with the phenology of their coniferous habitats. An incubation temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C] is a critical determinant of embryonic development rate; deviations from this thermal optimum prolong the incubation period and reduce hatching success. Similarly, the active metabolic temperature of approximately 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C] that characterizes the foraging adult during peak activity governs the timing of key post-hatching events such as fledging at 19 days since birth [tx = 19 days since birth] and the attainment of puberty at 57 days since birth [tp = 57 days since birth]. The species' reproductive output, with clutches of 7 to 11 eggs [N_R_i = clutches of 7 to 11 eggs], underscores a strategy that balances fecundity against the limited availability of caterpillar prey in early spring. The capacity for a single annual brood [F_R_i = single annual brood], combined with a high adult survival rate, shapes the overall life history of this resilient endemic of Eurasian woodlands.
